lessons.title: Be: am, is and are
baseline_goals: Use am, is and are with the right subject.
Make negative sentences and questions with be.
Distinguish a description from an action verb.
Complete a gap with the missing phrase only.

sections.title: Core rule / Meaning
sections.markdown: We use *be* to tell who or what someone/something is, or to describe how/where they are. For beginner sentences, choose the correct form for the subject.

sections.title: When to use
sections.markdown:
- **Name/identity:** She is my sister.
- **Feeling/description:** She is happy.
- **Place:** They are in the library.
- Distinguish *be* used with descriptions from an action verb in simple examples: *She is happy* versus *She plays*.

sections.title: Formulas / patterns
sections.markdown:
| Purpose | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Affirmative | **I am... / He, she, it is... / You, we, they are...** + (name / feeling / place / age) | I am eleven. / They are students. |
| Negative | Subject + **am/is/are + not** + (name / feeling / place / age / description) | He isn't late. / We aren't tired. |
| Yes/no question | **Am / Is / Are + subject** + (ready / here / a student)? | Are you ready? |
| Short answer | **Yes/No + subject + matching am/is/are** (add **not** for negative) | Yes, I am. |

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.markdown:
- *I am eleven. She is my sister. They are students.* → The subject determines **am/is/are**.
- *He isn't late. We aren't tired.* → Put **not** after *be* to make a negative.
- *Are you ready? Yes, I am.* → In a yes/no question, put *be* before the subject.
- *The books ___ on the desk.* → Write **are**, not the whole sentence, when the task asks for the missing word only.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.markdown:
- *She are happy* ✗ → *She is happy* ✓ (singular subject agreement).
- *Does she is ready?* ✗ → *Is she ready?* ✓ (do not add **do/does** to a basic *be* question).
- In a gap-fill, typing *The books are on the desk* instead of **are** may violate the exercise format even though the whole sentence is grammatical. A format issue must not automatically be labelled the same as a grammar misconception.

sections.title: Remember
sections.markdown: Learn *I am / he–she–it is / you–we–they are* first. For simple questions with *be*, put the form of *be* before the subject.

sections.title: Vietnamese Support (opt-in)
sections.markdown: *Động từ “be” đổi theo chủ ngữ: I am; he/she/it is; you/we/they are. Khi hỏi, đưa am/is/are lên trước chủ ngữ. Khi làm bài điền khuyết, chỉ nhập phần còn thiếu nếu đề yêu cầu.*

lessons.title: Choosing future forms: will, going to and present continuous
baseline_goals: Use will for spontaneous decisions and simple predictions.
Use be going to for prior intentions and predictions based on present evidence.
Use the present continuous for arranged future plans with a clear time or other arrangement detail.

sections.title: Core rule / Meaning
sections.markdown: More than one English form can refer to the future. Choose the one that best matches the information and intent in the situation; these are useful tendencies, **not absolute one-to-one rules**.

sections.title: When to use
sections.markdown:
| Form | Typical meaning in this lesson | Context cue | Worked example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **will + base verb** | Spontaneous decision / offer at the moment of speaking; also some predictions | The decision is made now | The phone is ringing — **I'll answer** it. |
| **am/is/are going to + base verb** | A prior intention or a prediction based on clear current evidence | Already planned, or evidence visible now | **I'm going to save** for a new bike. / Look at those clouds — **it's going to rain**. |
| **am/is/are + verb-ing** | A future arrangement already organised | Appointment, agreed time or other arrangement detail | **I'm meeting** Mai at four. |

sections.title: Formulas / patterns
sections.markdown:
- **Will:** Subject + **will + base verb** → *I will answer it.*
- **Going to:** Subject + **am/is/are + going to + base verb** → *She is going to practise tonight.*
- **Present continuous for an arrangement:** Subject + **am/is/are + verb-ing** (+ future arrangement context) → *We're seeing the film at 7 p.m.*

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.markdown:
- *The phone is ringing — **I'll answer** it.* → A decision made at the moment of speaking.
- *I'm going to save for a new bike.* → A previously formed intention.
- *Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.* → Present evidence motivates the prediction.
- *I'm meeting Mai at four.* → An existing arrangement, with a clear time.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.markdown:
- *I will answering it* ✗ → *I will answer it* ✓ (base form after **will**).
- *She going to practise tonight* ✗ → *She is going to practise tonight* ✓ (include appropriate **be**).
- *I am meet Mai at four* ✗ → *I am meeting Mai at four* ✓ (**be + -ing**).
- A whole grammatically correct sentence entered in a “write only the missing phrase” box is a **format mismatch**, not necessarily a grammar error.

sections.title: Quick decision guide
sections.markdown:
- Deciding right now? → **will** is often a good choice.
- Intention existed before speaking, or clear evidence now? → **going to** is often a good choice.
- Specific future arrangement already agreed? → **present continuous** is often a good choice.
- Ask: What does the full situation tell us? Without context, forms can overlap.

sections.title: Vietnamese Support (opt-in)
sections.markdown: *Will: quyết định/lời đề nghị ngay khi nói. Be going to: dự định đã có hoặc dự đoán dựa vào dấu hiệu. Hiện tại tiếp diễn: lịch hẹn/kế hoạch đã sắp xếp. Đây là xu hướng thường gặp, không phải ba quy tắc tuyệt đối loại trừ nhau.*

lessons.title: Defining and non-defining relative clauses
baseline_goals: Distinguish defining relative clauses from non-defining clauses that add extra information.
Use commas and who/which correctly in non-defining relative clauses.
Recognize when an object relative pronoun can be omitted in a defining clause.

sections.title: Core rule / Meaning
sections.markdown: Some relative clauses identify **which** person/thing we mean (*defining*). Others add extra information about an already identified person/thing (*non-defining*).

sections.title: When to use
sections.markdown:
| Type | Meaning | Punctuation | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Defining** | Identifies the intended person/thing; information is needed to identify it | Normally no commas | The student **who won the prize** is in my class. |
| **Non-defining** | Gives extra information about someone/something already identified | Set the extra clause off with commas | My aunt, **who lives in Hue**, is visiting us. |

sections.title: Relative words and omission
sections.markdown:
- **who** refers to a person; **which** refers to a thing. In a **non-defining clause**, do **not** use **that** instead of **who/which**.
- In a **defining clause**, *that* may be possible for people or things in relevant contexts, subject to clause constraints..
- **Object relative pronoun** in a defining clause may sometimes be omitted: *The film (that) we watched was excellent* → *The film we watched was excellent*.
- **Subject relative pronoun** should not be omitted in that structure: *The student who won the prize...*; not *The student won the prize is...*.
- **Non-defining relative clause:** **Never omit the relative pronoun**, whether it functions as a subject or an object. The option to omit an object relative pronoun applies **only to defining clauses** (and only in the relevant grammatical environment).

sections.title: Worked examples
sections.markdown:
- *The student who won the prize is in my class.* → The clause tells us **which student**.
- *My aunt, who lives in Hue, is visiting us.* → The relative clause adds information about *my aunt*.
- *This camera, which I bought last year, still works well.* → **which** adds information about *this camera*; commas mark the extra clause.
- *The film we watched was excellent.* → Object relative pronoun is omitted in a defining clause.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.markdown:
- *My aunt, that lives in Hue, is visiting us* ✗ → *My aunt, who lives in Hue, is visiting us* ✓ (non-defining clause: not **that**).
- *The student won the prize is in my class* ✗ → *The student who won the prize is in my class* ✓ (cannot omit subject relative pronoun there).
- Treat commas as **meaningful** in this lesson: do not assume defining and non-defining uses are interchangeable.

sections.title: Remember
sections.markdown: First ask whether the relative clause *identifies which one* or *adds extra information*. Then choose punctuation and pronoun accordingly. Never omit a relative pronoun in a non-defining clause; in a defining clause, only an object relative pronoun may sometimes be omitted.

sections.title: Vietnamese Support (opt-in)
sections.markdown: *Mệnh đề xác định giúp chỉ rõ người/vật và thường không có dấu phẩy; đôi khi có thể bỏ đại từ quan hệ làm tân ngữ. Mệnh đề không xác định chỉ bổ sung thông tin, có dấu phẩy, không dùng “that” và **không được lược bỏ đại từ quan hệ**.*
